newsitem.title: UK: Four accused of killing N.Ireland policeman.
newsitem.headline: Four accused of killing N.Ireland policeman.

text.p: Northern Ireland police charged four men on Wednesday with murdering an off-duty policeman who was kicked to death by a mob on Sunday, a spokesman said.
The killing, blamed by media reports on pro-British Protestants, intensified tension in the province which has been shaken recently by rival guerrilla violence and sectarian bitterness.
Police said the four would be brought before a court in Coleraine. Others were still being questioned about the murder, the spokesman added.
Gregory Taylor (41), a father of three, was set upon in a street in the town of Ballymoney by a mob angry that police had banned Protestant parades from a nearby Catholic village, media reports said.
The province's majority Protestants strongly support rule from London. The Catholic minority want an all-Ireland state ruled from Dublin.

On Tuesday Britain outlawed two guerrilla groups, the pro-British Loyalist Volunteer Force (LVF) and the pro-Irish Continuity Army Council (CAC), that have fuelled instability by a wave of bombings and shootings.
The ban came as mainstream Protestant and Catholic parties made a new bid to end years of conflict during talks that resumed in Belfast after a three month break for Britain's May 1 general election.
Chairman George Mitchell, a former U.S.senator who held round-table talks in Belfast on Tuesday, will hold another session next Tuesday. Bilateral discussions will continue in the meantime.

Clouded by increased violence by the Irish Republican Army, which seeks to end British rule of the province and attacks by outlawed Protestant militias, the talks have made little headway over the past 10 months.
Britain and Ireland say that the IRA must abandon violence before its political wing Sinn Fein can be invited to the talks.

The policeman's killing, the latest in a series of street attacks by Protestant and Catholic gangs, has increased fears about the potential for violence during contentious pro-British parades over the next few weeks.
